summary: This program stores a decimal number in a float and a more precise decimal in a double, then shows what happens when the two are mixed in arithmetic and when a double is forced back into a float.

lines.text: A float holds about seven significant digits. The trailing f is required, because Java treats a plain decimal literal as a double and will not silently squeeze it into a float.
A double uses twice the memory and holds roughly fifteen significant digits, which is why it is the default choice for decimal numbers in Java.
Joining a number to a string with + converts the number to text so it can be printed.

lines.code: double sum = f + d;              // float promoted to double
lines.text: When a float and a double meet in the same expression, Java widens the float to a double first, so the result is a double and no precision is lost.

lines.code: float narrowed = (float) d;      // explicit cast from double to float
lines.text: Going from double to float discards precision, so Java demands the explicit (float) cast as proof that you accept the loss.
The printed value shows the truncated digits, making the cost of narrowing visible.
